rows.evidence: Both versions preserve all seven concerns, four suggestions, and their boundaries, including explicit-ref pinning, canonical model aliases, the legacy typed-value fallback, UUID-named smoke output, per-lookup cached live status, and offline behavior. A's neutral overview and issue/fix tables are easier to scan than B's dense bullets, finding IDs, and synthetic result framing.
Both retain the canonical-alias defect, the pinned-snapshot scope, and the marked source-derived fallback. A scans better as a titled comment; B reads more naturally as compact prose.

Both cover explicit branch and tag refs, stable IDs and provenance URLs, one-time network resolution to a commit SHA, and network-free replay from the stored immutable ref. A has stronger visual structure; B is equally complete and more conversational.

Both preserve the pre-conversion failure, shared top-level parser, offline entry-point test, and defaults coverage. A's explicit title and two-item action list make the separate code and verification requests easier to retain.

Both retain populated-value scope, finite metric-rule validation before construction, the publication impact, and routing invalid rows to SourceConversionResult. A separates the actions for recall; B is smoother without losing content.

Both explicitly preserve pinned prompt content for new snapshots and an unset typed value plus missing-content marker for legacy snapshots. A states the complete defect and two-era remedy more naturally and with less scaffolding.
Both preserve live-only querying and unchanged offline behavior. A is more exact about present-null vendored entries; B expresses the same cached-missing case more plainly.

Both retain collision risk and unique-ownership gating for normalized spellings. A states the required precedence more decisively: exact canonical IDs must win first, rather than merely being preferred.

Both preserve all five findings and their strict boundaries, including the raw identity source, finite-number worker accounting, successful write and route transitions, exclusions-only reporting, and multi-route mid-write tests for the rollback path. B's severity/location/issue/fix table is more compact and easier to compare than A's long bullets and finding IDs.

Both retain preflight, recoverable prior files, the requirement that every new write and route transition succeed, and mid-write tests across several model routes specifically covering rollback. B's three action bullets materially improve recall.

Both preserve the alias-redirect identity instability, raw dataset model path as the identity input, and reconciled repository for metadata and routing. A communicates the same model-alias boundary more directly and with less repetition.

Both retain exclusions-only and fully clean runs, stale-report risk, atomic replacement after successful publication, and preservation of the last complete report. B's defect title makes the triggering condition immediately scannable without adding material noise.

Both preserve the PR #221 prerequisite and post-rebase default-rich CLI check, the exact guide path and all three documentation limits, and every optional suggestion's conditions. A's neutral summary and separated issue/fix tables are easier to scan than B's dense bullets and run framing; merge judgment itself is not rewarded.

Both retain why warnings are hidden, PR #221 as the prerequisite, the after-rebase condition, and a default-rich CLI check of the complete path. A is more compact and natural; B's four short blocks over-segment one straightforward finding.

Both preserve the exact required guide path and require coverage of the alias trigger, warning-only result, and single-record evidence limit. A delivers the same complete request more directly; B repeats the missing-guide point in both heading and body.
